Day 60 of 100 · Networking Deep Dive

Network Troubleshooting Sequence

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityNetworking Deep DivePublished artifact recovered

Troubleshooting becomes repeatable when a failed request is traced through DNS, routing, transport, TLS, proxy, backend and system pressure one layer at a time.

Architecture / mental model

DNS → route → port/transport → TLS → HTTP/proxy → backend/dependencies → disk

How it works

Start with the name. If DNS is wrong, testing the application at the expected hostname is already testing the wrong destination. Next prove the route and whether the target port is reachable/listening.

Only after transport works should TLS and HTTP behavior become the focus. Proxy logs, application logs and backend dependency checks then narrow failures inside the service path.

System pressure belongs in the sequence too. Full filesystems or inodes can break logging, temporary files, databases and deployments even when the network path itself is healthy.

Hands-on reference

dig +short core-shield.enthernetservice.com
ip route get DEST_IP
traceroute DEST_IP
nc -vz DEST_IP 443
openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST
curl -v https://HOST
df -h
df -i
sudo du -xhd1 /var | sort -h
sudo lsof +L1

Verification

For one incident or lab failure, write down the observation at every layer and stop as soon as the first layer fails. Repair it, then continue from that layer forward.

Field note / gotcha

`df` can show space consumed that `du` cannot find when a process still holds a deleted file open. `lsof +L1` is the clue.

Security considerations

Troubleshooting commands and logs can expose internal addresses, headers and secrets. Collect the minimum evidence needed and protect incident artifacts.

What I learned

Prove one layer, record the evidence, then move to the next.
